CHAPTER 30 - INTEGRATION

Introduction

Differentiation answers the question: given a function, what is its rate of change? Integration answers the reverse question: given the rate of change (the derivative), what is the original function? For this reason integration is called the INVERSE operation of differentiation, and the result is called an ANTIDERIVATIVE or INDEFINITE INTEGRAL. Integration is one of the two central ideas of calculus. It lets us recover a function from its derivative, and it lets us add up (integrate) infinitely many small quantities to find areas, volumes, lengths and totals. This chapter builds the machinery of INDEFINITE integration: the meaning of the antiderivative and the constant of integration, a table of standard integrals, the algebraic properties of the integral, and the three great methods - substitution, integration by parts, and partial fractions - together with a set of special standard integrals and the integration of trigonometric functions. Worked examples run throughout.

30.1 INTEGRATION AS THE INVERSE OF DIFFERENTIATION

If a function F(x) has derivative f(x), that is d/dx [F(x)] = f(x), then F(x) is called an ANTIDERIVATIVE (or primitive, or integral) of f(x). We write

   integral f(x) dx = F(x) + C

Here the symbol integral is the integral sign, f(x) is the INTEGRAND, dx shows that x is the variable of integration, and C is an arbitrary constant called the CONSTANT OF INTEGRATION. For example, since d/dx (x^2) = 2x, an antiderivative of 2x is x^2, so integral 2x dx = x^2 + C. Because d/dx (x^2 + 5) = 2x as well, and indeed d/dx (x^2 + C) = 2x for ANY constant C, the antiderivative is never unique: any two antiderivatives of the same function differ only by a constant. That is why we always add + C to an indefinite integral. Geometrically, integral f(x) dx represents a whole FAMILY of curves y = F(x) + C, one for each value of C, all having the same slope f(x) at every value of x - a family of parallel curves.

The indefinite integral is INDEFINITE precisely because of this unknown constant. (A DEFINITE integral, with limits, produces a definite number and the constant cancels.) To check any integration result, simply differentiate the answer: if you get back the integrand, the integration is correct.

30.2 STANDARD INTEGRALS

By reversing the standard derivatives we obtain a table of standard integrals. The most important are:

   integral x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C,   provided n is not equal to -1
   integral (1/x) dx = log |x| + C
   integral e^x dx = e^x + C
   integral a^x dx = a^x / log a + C   (a > 0, a not equal to 1)
   integral sin x dx = - cos x + C
   integral cos x dx = sin x + C
   integral sec^2 x dx = tan x + C
   integral cosec^2 x dx = - cot x + C
   integral sec x tan x dx = sec x + C
   integral cosec x cot x dx = - cosec x + C
   integral (1/sqrt(1 - x^2)) dx = sin^-1 x + C
   integral (1/(1 + x^2)) dx = tan^-1 x + C

The power rule integral x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C is the workhorse. It fails only for n = -1 (division by zero); that single case is covered separately by integral (1/x) dx = log |x| + C. As a first worked example, integral x^3 dx = x^4/4 + C, and integral (1/x^2) dx = integral x^-2 dx = x^-1/(-1) + C = -1/x + C. Also integral sqrt(x) dx = integral x^(1/2) dx = x^(3/2)/(3/2) + C = (2/3) x^(3/2) + C, and integral 1 dx = x + C.

30.3 PROPERTIES OF THE INDEFINITE INTEGRAL

Integration is linear. Two rules follow directly from the linearity of differentiation:

Property 1 (constant multiple): integral k f(x) dx = k integral f(x) dx, where k is a constant. A constant factor may be taken outside the integral sign.

Property 2 (sum and difference): integral [f(x) + g(x)] dx = integral f(x) dx + integral g(x) dx, and likewise for a difference. The integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals.

These let us integrate any polynomial term by term. For instance,

   integral (3x^2 + 4x - 5) dx = 3 (x^3/3) + 4 (x^2/2) - 5x + C = x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x + C.

Note that we write only ONE constant C for the whole expression. Also note that, unlike differentiation, there is NO simple product rule or quotient rule for integration - the integral of a product is NOT the product of the integrals. Products and quotients are handled by the special methods that follow.

30.4 INTEGRATION BY SUBSTITUTION (CHANGE OF VARIABLE)

Many integrals become standard once we change the variable. In the method of SUBSTITUTION we replace part of the integrand by a new variable t so that the integral turns into a standard form. If we put x = g(t), then dx = g'(t) dt, and

   integral f(x) dx = integral f(g(t)) g'(t) dt.

The key idea: choose the substitution so that its derivative already appears (up to a constant) in the integrand. A very useful special case is

   integral [f'(x) / f(x)] dx = log |f(x)| + C,

because putting t = f(x) gives dt = f'(x) dx, and the integral becomes integral dt/t = log |t| + C.

Worked example 1: integral (2x) / (x^2 + 1) dx. Put t = x^2 + 1, so dt = 2x dx. The integral becomes integral dt/t = log |t| + C = log (x^2 + 1) + C.

Worked example 2: integral cos(3x) dx. Put t = 3x, dt = 3 dx, so dx = dt/3. Then integral cos t (dt/3) = (1/3) sin t + C = (1/3) sin 3x + C. In general integral cos(ax + b) dx = (1/a) sin(ax + b) + C.

Worked example 3: integral sin^4 x cos x dx. Put t = sin x, dt = cos x dx. Then integral t^4 dt = t^5/5 + C = (sin^5 x)/5 + C.

Worked example 4: integral tan x dx = integral (sin x / cos x) dx. Put t = cos x, dt = - sin x dx, so integral (-dt/t) = - log |t| + C = - log |cos x| + C = log |sec x| + C. Similarly integral cot x dx = log |sin x| + C.

30.5 INTEGRATION BY PARTS

When the integrand is a PRODUCT of two functions of different types, we use INTEGRATION BY PARTS, which comes from reversing the product rule of differentiation. The formula is

   integral u dv = u v - integral v du,

or, writing u = u(x) and dv = v'(x) dx,

   integral u v' dx = u v - integral v u' dx.

The art lies in choosing which factor is u (to be differentiated) and which is dv (to be integrated). A helpful guide is the ILATE rule: choose u as the function that comes FIRST in the order

   I - Inverse trigonometric
   L - Logarithmic
   A - Algebraic (powers of x)
   T - Trigonometric
   E - Exponential

Whatever remains, together with dx, is dv.

Worked example 1: integral x e^x dx. Take u = x (Algebraic, before Exponential) and dv = e^x dx, so du = dx and v = e^x. Then integral x e^x dx = x e^x - integral e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + C = e^x (x - 1) + C.

Worked example 2: integral x cos x dx. Take u = x, dv = cos x dx, so du = dx, v = sin x. Then integral x cos x dx = x sin x - integral sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C.

Worked example 3: integral log x dx. Write it as integral (log x)(1) dx with u = log x (Logarithmic) and dv = dx, so du = (1/x) dx, v = x. Then integral log x dx = x log x - integral x (1/x) dx = x log x - integral 1 dx = x log x - x + C.

A useful standard result that follows from integration by parts is

   integral e^x [f(x) + f'(x)] dx = e^x f(x) + C.

30.6 INTEGRATION BY PARTIAL FRACTIONS

To integrate a RATIONAL function P(x)/Q(x) (a ratio of polynomials) where the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator, we first split the fraction into a sum of simpler PARTIAL FRACTIONS, and then integrate each piece. (If the numerator's degree is not smaller, divide first.) The form of the partial fractions depends on the factors of the denominator:

   px + q / [(x - a)(x - b)]  =  A/(x - a) + B/(x - b)     (distinct linear factors)
   px + q / (x - a)^2         =  A/(x - a) + B/(x - a)^2    (repeated linear factor)
   and an irreducible quadratic factor (x^2 + bx + c) contributes a term (Ax + B)/(x^2 + bx + c).

Worked example: integral dx / (x^2 - 1) = integral dx / [(x - 1)(x + 1)]. Write

   1 / [(x - 1)(x + 1)] = A/(x - 1) + B/(x + 1).

Multiplying out: 1 = A(x + 1) + B(x - 1). Putting x = 1 gives 1 = 2A, so A = 1/2. Putting x = -1 gives 1 = -2B, so B = -1/2. Hence

   integral dx/(x^2 - 1) = (1/2) integral dx/(x - 1) - (1/2) integral dx/(x + 1)
        = (1/2) log |x - 1| - (1/2) log |x + 1| + C = (1/2) log |(x - 1)/(x + 1)| + C.

This is the general pattern: resolve, then integrate each simple fraction using integral dx/(x - a) = log |x - a| + C.

30.7 SPECIAL INTEGRALS (STANDARD RESULTS)

Certain integrals involving quadratics occur so often that their results are memorised as standard formulae:

   integral dx / (x^2 + a^2) = (1/a) tan^-1 (x/a) + C
   integral dx / (x^2 - a^2) = (1/2a) log |(x - a)/(x + a)| + C
   integral dx / (a^2 - x^2) = (1/2a) log |(a + x)/(a - x)| + C
   integral dx / sqrt(x^2 + a^2) = log |x + sqrt(x^2 + a^2)| + C
   integral dx / sqrt(x^2 - a^2) = log |x + sqrt(x^2 - a^2)| + C
   integral dx / sqrt(a^2 - x^2) = sin^-1 (x/a) + C

Worked example 1: integral dx/(x^2 + 9). Here a^2 = 9, so a = 3, and the integral is (1/3) tan^-1 (x/3) + C.

Worked example 2: integral dx/sqrt(4 - x^2). Here a^2 = 4, a = 2, giving sin^-1 (x/2) + C.

To use these forms when the quadratic is not already a pure sum of squares, we COMPLETE THE SQUARE. For example x^2 + 4x + 13 = (x + 2)^2 + 9, so integral dx/(x^2 + 4x + 13) = integral dx/[(x + 2)^2 + 3^2] = (1/3) tan^-1 [(x + 2)/3] + C.

30.8 INTEGRATION OF TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS

Trigonometric integrands are handled using identities that turn products and powers into sums, which are then integrated term by term.

(a) Powers of sin and cos using half-angle identities:
   sin^2 x = (1 - cos 2x)/2,   cos^2 x = (1 + cos 2x)/2.
So integral sin^2 x dx = integral (1 - cos 2x)/2 dx = (1/2)[x - (sin 2x)/2] + C = x/2 - (sin 2x)/4 + C. Similarly integral cos^2 x dx = x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + C.

(b) Products of sines and cosines using product-to-sum identities, for example
   2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A - B).
So integral 2 sin 3x cos x dx = integral [sin 4x + sin 2x] dx = - (cos 4x)/4 - (cos 2x)/2 + C.

(c) Odd powers by substitution: for integral sin^3 x dx write sin^3 x = sin x (1 - cos^2 x); put t = cos x to get integral -(1 - t^2) dt = - t + t^3/3 + C = - cos x + (cos^3 x)/3 + C.

These techniques, combined with the standard integrals and the three methods, let us integrate a very wide range of functions. The single most valuable habit is to VERIFY every answer by differentiating it: the derivative of a correct indefinite integral is exactly the original integrand.

SUMMARY

- Integration is the inverse of differentiation. If d/dx F(x) = f(x) then integral f(x) dx = F(x) + C, where C is the arbitrary constant of integration; antiderivatives of a function differ only by a constant, giving a family of parallel curves.
- Standard integrals: integral x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C (n not -1); integral (1/x) dx = log |x| + C; integral e^x dx = e^x + C; integral a^x dx = a^x/log a + C; integral sin x dx = - cos x + C; integral cos x dx = sin x + C; integral sec^2 x dx = tan x + C.
- Properties: integral k f dx = k integral f dx and integral (f +/- g) dx = integral f dx +/- integral g dx; there is no product or quotient rule for integration.
- Substitution: put t = g(x) so that dt appears in the integrand; special case integral f'(x)/f(x) dx = log |f(x)| + C.
- Integration by parts: integral u dv = uv - integral v du, choosing u by the ILATE order (Inverse trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential); e.g. integral log x dx = x log x - x + C.
- Partial fractions: split a proper rational function into simple fractions over its linear/quadratic factors, then integrate each using integral dx/(x - a) = log |x - a| + C.
- Special integrals: integral dx/(x^2 + a^2) = (1/a) tan^-1(x/a) + C; integral dx/(x^2 - a^2) = (1/2a) log |(x - a)/(x + a)| + C; integral dx/sqrt(a^2 - x^2) = sin^-1(x/a) + C; integral dx/sqrt(x^2 + a^2) = log |x + sqrt(x^2 + a^2)| + C; complete the square first when needed.
- Trigonometric integrals: use half-angle and product-to-sum identities and substitution to reduce powers and products; always check a result by differentiating it.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Integration (NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show full working for each integration and remember to add the constant of integration C to every indefinite integral. Verify your answers by differentiation where possible.

questions.question: Define an antiderivative and explain, with the example integral 2x dx, why an arbitrary constant of integration must be added.
questions.answer:
A function F(x) is an antiderivative of f(x) if d/dx F(x) = f(x). The indefinite integral integral f(x) dx = F(x) + C is the general antiderivative.

For f(x) = 2x: since d/dx (x^2) = 2x, one antiderivative is x^2. But d/dx (x^2 + C) = 2x for ANY constant C, so x^2 + 1, x^2 - 7 and so on are all antiderivatives of 2x. Any two antiderivatives differ only by a constant, so we write

   integral 2x dx = x^2 + C.

The + C represents this whole family of curves; without it the answer would be incomplete.
questions.explanation: Definition + why C is needed (antiderivatives differ by a constant).

questions.question: Evaluate integral (3x^2 + 4x - 5 + 1/x) dx.
questions.answer:
Integrate term by term using linearity and the power rule:

   integral 3x^2 dx = 3 (x^3/3) = x^3
   integral 4x dx = 4 (x^2/2) = 2x^2
   integral (-5) dx = -5x
   integral (1/x) dx = log |x|

Adding, integral (3x^2 + 4x - 5 + 1/x) dx = x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x + log |x| + C.
questions.explanation: Term-by-term power rule plus integral(1/x) = log|x|.

questions.question: Evaluate integral 2x sqrt(x^2 + 1) dx by substitution.
questions.answer:
Put t = x^2 + 1, so dt = 2x dx. The integral becomes

   integral sqrt(t) dt = integral t^(1/2) dt = t^(3/2)/(3/2) + C = (2/3) t^(3/2) + C.

Replacing t = x^2 + 1:

   integral 2x sqrt(x^2 + 1) dx = (2/3) (x^2 + 1)^(3/2) + C.
questions.explanation: Substitution t = x^2 + 1 gives dt = 2x dx.

questions.question: Evaluate integral tan x dx.
questions.answer:
Write tan x = sin x / cos x. Put t = cos x, so dt = - sin x dx, i.e. sin x dx = - dt. Then

   integral (sin x / cos x) dx = integral (-dt)/t = - log |t| + C = - log |cos x| + C.

Since - log |cos x| = log |sec x|, we may also write integral tan x dx = log |sec x| + C.
questions.explanation: Substitution t = cos x; form integral f'/f.

questions.question: Using integration by parts, evaluate integral x e^x dx and integral log x dx. State the ILATE rule you used.
questions.answer:
ILATE rule: when integrating a product, choose u as the function that appears first in the order Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential.

(i) integral x e^x dx: x is Algebraic, e^x is Exponential, so take u = x and dv = e^x dx. Then du = dx, v = e^x.
   integral x e^x dx = u v - integral v du = x e^x - integral e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + C = e^x (x - 1) + C.

(ii) integral log x dx: write it as integral (log x)(1) dx. Log is chosen as u, and dv = dx. Then du = (1/x) dx, v = x.
   integral log x dx = x log x - integral x (1/x) dx = x log x - integral 1 dx = x log x - x + C.
questions.explanation: Parts with ILATE: u = x then u = log x.

questions.question: Evaluate integral dx/(x^2 - 1) by the method of partial fractions, showing all steps.
questions.answer:
Factor the denominator: x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1). Write

   1 / [(x - 1)(x + 1)] = A/(x - 1) + B/(x + 1).

Multiply both sides by (x - 1)(x + 1):

   1 = A(x + 1) + B(x - 1).

Put x = 1: 1 = A(2), so A = 1/2. Put x = -1: 1 = B(-2), so B = -1/2. Therefore

   integral dx/(x^2 - 1) = (1/2) integral dx/(x - 1) - (1/2) integral dx/(x + 1)
        = (1/2) log |x - 1| - (1/2) log |x + 1| + C
        = (1/2) log |(x - 1)/(x + 1)| + C.
questions.explanation: Resolve into A/(x-1) + B/(x+1); integrate each log.

questions.question: Evaluate integral dx/(x^2 + 9).
questions.answer:
This matches the standard form integral dx/(x^2 + a^2) = (1/a) tan^-1 (x/a) + C. Here a^2 = 9, so a = 3. Therefore

   integral dx/(x^2 + 9) = (1/3) tan^-1 (x/3) + C.

questions.question: Evaluate integral dx/(x^2 + 4x + 13) by completing the square.
questions.answer:

Put t = x^2 + 3x + 5, so dt = (2x + 3) dx. Then

   integral (2x + 3)/(x^2 + 3x + 5) dx = integral dt/t = log |t| + C = log |x^2 + 3x + 5| + C.

Method: substitution using the special case integral f'(x)/f(x) dx = log |f(x)| + C, chosen because the numerator is the exact derivative of the denominator.

Explain why integral f(x) dx is called an indefinite integral and involves a constant C.
questions.answer: It is called indefinite because it is not a single function but a whole family of functions F(x) + C, one for each value of the arbitrary constant C. Since any two antiderivatives of f(x) differ only by a constant (because the derivative of a constant is zero), the general antiderivative must include + C. This constant is undetermined unless extra information (an initial condition) is given, which is why the integral is 'indefinite'.
questions.explanation: Antiderivatives differ by a constant; C undetermined.

The curve passes through (1, 3): 3 = 1^2 + C, so C = 2.

Therefore y = x^2 + 2.

questions.question: Evaluate integral x sin x dx using integration by parts.
questions.answer:
Take u = x (algebraic), dv = sin x dx. Then du = dx, v = - cos x. By parts:

   integral x sin x dx = u v - integral v du = - x cos x - integral (- cos x) dx
        = - x cos x + integral cos x dx = - x cos x + sin x + C.
questions.explanation: Parts with u = x, v = -cos x.

questions.question: Evaluate integral x^2 log x dx.

   integral x^2 log x dx = (x^3/3) log x - integral (x^3/3)(1/x) dx
        = (x^3/3) log x - (1/3) integral x^2 dx
        = (x^3/3) log x - (1/3)(x^3/3) + C = (x^3/3) log x - x^3/9 + C.
questions.explanation: Parts with u = log x, dv = x^2 dx.

questions.question: Evaluate integral tan^-1 x dx.

   integral tan^-1 x dx = x tan^-1 x - integral x/(1 + x^2) dx.

For the remaining integral put t = 1 + x^2, dt = 2x dx: integral x/(1 + x^2) dx = (1/2) log(1 + x^2). Hence

   integral tan^-1 x dx = x tan^-1 x - (1/2) log (1 + x^2) + C.
questions.explanation: Parts with u = tan^-1 x, then substitution.

questions.question: Explain integration as the inverse of differentiation. Define the antiderivative and the indefinite integral, and using integral 3x^2 dx illustrate the family of curves and the need for the constant of integration.
questions.answer:
Differentiation gives the rate of change of a function; integration reverses this to recover the function from its derivative. If d/dx F(x) = f(x), then F(x) is called an antiderivative (or primitive) of f(x), and the indefinite integral is written integral f(x) dx = F(x) + C.

For f(x) = 3x^2: since d/dx (x^3) = 3x^2, an antiderivative is x^3. But d/dx (x^3 + C) = 3x^2 for every constant C, so

   integral 3x^2 dx = x^3 + C.

Family of curves: the equation y = x^3 + C describes infinitely many curves, one for each value of C (for example x^3, x^3 + 1, x^3 - 4). They are vertical translates of one another and all have the same slope 3x^2 at each x, so they are 'parallel'. Because differentiation destroys the constant term, integration cannot recover it; the arbitrary constant C represents this lost information. To pin down a single curve we need an extra condition, e.g. a point the curve passes through. Any integration can be checked by differentiating the answer to recover the integrand.
questions.explanation: Inverse relation; antiderivative; integral 3x^2 = x^3 + C; parallel curves; role of C.

questions.question: State the two linearity properties of integration and use them to evaluate integral (x^3 - 6x^2 + 4x - 7 + 2/x) dx. Verify part of your answer by differentiation.
questions.answer:
Linearity properties:
1. Constant multiple: integral k f(x) dx = k integral f(x) dx.
2. Sum/difference: integral [f(x) +/- g(x)] dx = integral f(x) dx +/- integral g(x) dx.

Applying term by term:
   integral x^3 dx = x^4/4
   integral (-6x^2) dx = -6 (x^3/3) = -2x^3
   integral 4x dx = 4 (x^2/2) = 2x^2
   integral (-7) dx = -7x
   integral (2/x) dx = 2 log |x|

Therefore
   integral (x^3 - 6x^2 + 4x - 7 + 2/x) dx = x^4/4 - 2x^3 + 2x^2 - 7x + 2 log |x| + C.

Verification: differentiate x^4/4 - 2x^3 + 2x^2 - 7x + 2 log |x|:
   d/dx = x^3 - 6x^2 + 4x - 7 + 2/x,
which is the original integrand. Hence the result is correct.
questions.explanation: Linearity; integrate term by term; differentiate back to check.

questions.question: Describe the method of integration by substitution. Use it to evaluate (a) integral 2x sqrt(x^2 + 1) dx and (b) integral tan x dx.
questions.answer:
Method: if a part of the integrand and its derivative both appear, we substitute t for that part. Putting t = g(x) gives dt = g'(x) dx, and integral f(x) dx becomes an integral in t that is a standard form; after integrating we replace t by g(x).

(a) integral 2x sqrt(x^2 + 1) dx. Put t = x^2 + 1, so dt = 2x dx. Then
   integral sqrt(t) dt = integral t^(1/2) dt = t^(3/2)/(3/2) = (2/3) t^(3/2).
Replacing t: integral 2x sqrt(x^2 + 1) dx = (2/3) (x^2 + 1)^(3/2) + C.

(b) integral tan x dx = integral (sin x / cos x) dx. Put t = cos x, so dt = - sin x dx, i.e. sin x dx = - dt. Then
   integral (sin x / cos x) dx = integral (- dt)/t = - log |t| + C = - log |cos x| + C = log |sec x| + C.
questions.explanation: Explain substitution; (a) t = x^2+1; (b) t = cos x.

questions.question: State the integration-by-parts formula and the ILATE rule. Use them to evaluate (a) integral x cos x dx and (b) integral x^2 e^x dx.
questions.answer:
Formula: integral u dv = uv - integral v du. ILATE rule for choosing u: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential (choose u as whichever type comes first).

(a) integral x cos x dx. u = x (Algebraic before Trig), dv = cos x dx; du = dx, v = sin x.
   integral x cos x dx = x sin x - integral sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C.

(b) integral x^2 e^x dx. u = x^2, dv = e^x dx; du = 2x dx, v = e^x.
   integral x^2 e^x dx = x^2 e^x - integral 2x e^x dx.
For integral 2x e^x dx apply parts again (u = 2x, dv = e^x dx): 2x e^x - integral 2 e^x dx = 2x e^x - 2 e^x.
So integral x^2 e^x dx = x^2 e^x - (2x e^x - 2 e^x) + C = e^x (x^2 - 2x + 2) + C.
questions.explanation: Parts formula + ILATE; (a) once; (b) parts applied twice.

questions.question: Explain the method of partial fractions and use it to evaluate integral (3x + 5)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)] dx.
questions.answer:
Method: a proper rational function P(x)/Q(x) (deg P < deg Q) is written as a sum of simpler fractions determined by the factors of Q(x); distinct linear factors (x - a), (x - b) give terms A/(x - a) + B/(x - b). We find A, B and integrate each simple fraction using integral dx/(x - a) = log |x - a| + C.

Write (3x + 5)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)] = A/(x - 1) + B/(x + 2). Then
   3x + 5 = A(x + 2) + B(x - 1).
Put x = 1: 3(1) + 5 = A(3), so 8 = 3A, A = 8/3.
Put x = -2: 3(-2) + 5 = B(-3), so -1 = -3B, B = 1/3.

Therefore
   integral (3x + 5)/[(x - 1)(x + 2)] dx = (8/3) integral dx/(x - 1) + (1/3) integral dx/(x + 2)
        = (8/3) log |x - 1| + (1/3) log |x + 2| + C.
questions.explanation: Resolve; A = 8/3, B = 1/3; integrate the two logs.

questions.question: Evaluate (a) integral dx/(x^2 + 4x + 8) and (b) integral dx/sqrt(x^2 + 4), stating the standard results used.
questions.answer:
(a) Complete the square: x^2 + 4x + 8 = (x + 2)^2 + 4 = (x + 2)^2 + 2^2. Using integral du/(u^2 + a^2) = (1/a) tan^-1(u/a) + C with u = x + 2, a = 2:
   integral dx/(x^2 + 4x + 8) = (1/2) tan^-1 [(x + 2)/2] + C.

(b) Use the standard result integral dx/sqrt(x^2 + a^2) = log |x + sqrt(x^2 + a^2)| + C with a^2 = 4, a = 2:
   integral dx/sqrt(x^2 + 4) = log |x + sqrt(x^2 + 4)| + C.
questions.explanation: (a) complete square + arctan; (b) standard log result.

questions.question: Integrate the following trigonometric functions, showing the identities used: (a) integral sin^2 x dx, (b) integral 2 sin 3x cos x dx, (c) integral sin^3 x dx.
questions.answer:
(a) sin^2 x = (1 - cos 2x)/2, so
   integral sin^2 x dx = (1/2) integral (1 - cos 2x) dx = (1/2)[x - (sin 2x)/2] + C = x/2 - (sin 2x)/4 + C.

(b) Use 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A - B): 2 sin 3x cos x = sin 4x + sin 2x. So
   integral 2 sin 3x cos x dx = integral (sin 4x + sin 2x) dx = - (cos 4x)/4 - (cos 2x)/2 + C.

(c) sin^3 x = sin x (1 - cos^2 x). Put t = cos x, dt = - sin x dx:
   integral sin^3 x dx = integral (1 - cos^2 x) sin x dx = integral (1 - t^2)(- dt) = - integral (1 - t^2) dt
        = - (t - t^3/3) + C = - cos x + (cos^3 x)/3 + C.

questions.answer:
(a) integral x e^x dx - integration by PARTS (algebraic times exponential). u = x, dv = e^x dx: = x e^x - integral e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + C = e^x (x - 1) + C.

(b) integral (2x + 1)/(x^2 + x + 1) dx - SUBSTITUTION, since d/dx (x^2 + x + 1) = 2x + 1 (the f'/f form). Put t = x^2 + x + 1, dt = (2x + 1) dx: = integral dt/t = log |t| + C = log |x^2 + x + 1| + C.

(c) integral dx/(x^2 - 16) - SPECIAL/standard integral with a = 4: integral dx/(x^2 - a^2) = (1/2a) log |(x - a)/(x + a)| + C, so = (1/8) log |(x - 4)/(x + 4)| + C.
questions.explanation: Choose parts / substitution / standard result respectively.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Integration reverses differentiation: if d/dx F(x) = f(x) then integral f(x) dx = F(x) + C. Because the derivative of any constant is zero, an antiderivative is determined only up to a constant, and the general integral includes the constant of integration C.
(a) What is meant by an antiderivative of f(x)?
(b) Why must a constant C be included in an indefinite integral?
(c) Find integral 4x^3 dx.
(d) If the curve y = F(x) with F'(x) = 4x^3 passes through (0, 5), find F(x).
questions.answer:
(a) An antiderivative of f(x) is a function F(x) whose derivative equals f(x), i.e. d/dx F(x) = f(x).
(b) Because two antiderivatives of the same function differ only by a constant (the derivative of a constant is zero), so the general answer must carry an arbitrary constant C.
(c) integral 4x^3 dx = 4 (x^4/4) + C = x^4 + C.
(d) F(x) = x^4 + C; F(0) = 0 + C = 5, so C = 5 and F(x) = x^4 + 5.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative; role of C; x^4 + C; use point for C.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Standard integrals are obtained by reversing standard derivatives: integral x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n not equal to -1, integral (1/x) dx = log |x| + C, integral e^x dx = e^x + C, integral sin x dx = - cos x + C.
(a) Why is the power rule not valid for n = -1?
(b) Evaluate integral x^5 dx.
(c) Evaluate integral (1/x) dx.
(d) Evaluate integral (e^x + sin x) dx.
questions.answer:
(a) For n = -1 the formula would divide by n + 1 = 0, which is undefined; that case is covered separately by integral (1/x) dx = log |x| + C.
(b) integral x^5 dx = x^6/6 + C.
(c) integral (1/x) dx = log |x| + C.
(d) integral (e^x + sin x) dx = e^x - cos x + C.
questions.explanation: n=-1 excluded; x^6/6; log|x|; e^x - cos x.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Integration is linear: integral k f(x) dx = k integral f(x) dx and integral [f(x) +/- g(x)] dx = integral f(x) dx +/- integral g(x) dx. These allow polynomials to be integrated term by term. There is, however, no product rule for integration.
(a) State the constant-multiple rule.
(b) Evaluate integral (6x^2 - 4x + 3) dx.
(c) Is integral (x cos x) dx equal to (integral x dx)(integral cos x dx)? Explain.
(d) Verify your answer to (b) by differentiation.
questions.answer:
(a) integral k f(x) dx = k integral f(x) dx: a constant factor may be moved outside the integral.
(b) integral (6x^2 - 4x + 3) dx = 6(x^3/3) - 4(x^2/2) + 3x + C = 2x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x + C.
(c) No. There is no product rule for integration, so the integral of a product is not the product of the integrals; integral x cos x dx must be found by parts (= x sin x + cos x + C).
(d) d/dx (2x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x) = 6x^2 - 4x + 3, the original integrand, confirming (b).
questions.explanation: Constant rule; term-by-term; no product rule; check by differentiating.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In substitution we set t = g(x) so that dt = g'(x) dx turns the integral into a standard form. A key special case is integral f'(x)/f(x) dx = log |f(x)| + C, used whenever the numerator is the derivative of the denominator.
(a) State the substitution to evaluate integral 2x/(x^2 + 5) dx.
(b) Evaluate that integral.
(c) Evaluate integral cos 5x dx.
(d) Evaluate integral sin^2 x cos x dx.
questions.answer:
(a) Put t = x^2 + 5, since dt = 2x dx appears in the numerator.
(b) integral 2x/(x^2 + 5) dx = integral dt/t = log |t| + C = log (x^2 + 5) + C.
(c) integral cos 5x dx = (1/5) sin 5x + C (put t = 5x).
(d) Put t = sin x, dt = cos x dx: integral t^2 dt = t^3/3 + C = (sin^3 x)/3 + C.
questions.explanation: t = x^2+5 gives log; cos5x -> (1/5)sin5x; t = sin x.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Integration by parts, integral u dv = uv - integral v du, comes from reversing the product rule. The factor u is chosen by the ILATE order: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential.
(a) For integral x e^x dx, which factor is u and why?
(b) Evaluate integral x e^x dx.
(c) Evaluate integral log x dx.
(d) Evaluate integral x sin x dx.
questions.answer:
(a) u = x, because Algebraic (A) comes before Exponential (E) in ILATE; dv = e^x dx.
(b) integral x e^x dx = x e^x - integral e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + C = e^x (x - 1) + C.
(c) Write integral (log x)(1) dx; u = log x, dv = dx, v = x: = x log x - integral x(1/x) dx = x log x - x + C.
(d) u = x, dv = sin x dx, v = - cos x: = - x cos x + integral cos x dx = - x cos x + sin x + C.
questions.explanation: ILATE choice; three worked parts integrals.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A proper rational function is integrated by resolving it into partial fractions. For distinct linear factors, 1/[(x - a)(x - b)] = A/(x - a) + B/(x - b); each simple fraction integrates to a logarithm.
(a) Resolve 1/[(x - 2)(x + 1)] into partial fractions.
(b) Hence evaluate integral dx/[(x - 2)(x + 1)].
(c) What condition on the degrees must hold before this method is applied?
(d) State the integral of 1/(x - a).
questions.answer:
(a) 1/[(x - 2)(x + 1)] = A/(x - 2) + B/(x + 1); so 1 = A(x + 1) + B(x - 2). Put x = 2: 1 = 3A, A = 1/3. Put x = -1: 1 = -3B, B = -1/3. Thus = (1/3)/(x - 2) - (1/3)/(x + 1).
(b) integral dx/[(x - 2)(x + 1)] = (1/3) log |x - 2| - (1/3) log |x + 1| + C = (1/3) log |(x - 2)/(x + 1)| + C.
(c) The numerator's degree must be less than the denominator's (a proper fraction); otherwise divide first.
(d) integral dx/(x - a) = log |x - a| + C.
questions.explanation: A = 1/3, B = -1/3; integrate to logs; proper-fraction condition.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Special integrals include integral dx/(x^2 + a^2) = (1/a) tan^-1(x/a) + C and integral dx/sqrt(a^2 - x^2) = sin^-1(x/a) + C. When the quadratic is not a pure square-sum, we complete the square first.
(a) Evaluate integral dx/(x^2 + 4).
(b) Evaluate integral dx/sqrt(25 - x^2).
(c) Write x^2 + 6x + 10 as a completed square.
(d) Hence evaluate integral dx/(x^2 + 6x + 10).
questions.answer:
(a) a = 2: integral dx/(x^2 + 4) = (1/2) tan^-1 (x/2) + C.
(b) a = 5: integral dx/sqrt(25 - x^2) = sin^-1 (x/5) + C.
(c) x^2 + 6x + 10 = (x + 3)^2 + 1.
(d) With u = x + 3, a = 1: integral dx/(x^2 + 6x + 10) = tan^-1 (x + 3) + C.
questions.explanation: arctan and arcsin forms; complete square to (x+3)^2+1.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Trigonometric integrands are simplified with identities: sin^2 x = (1 - cos 2x)/2, cos^2 x = (1 + cos 2x)/2, and 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A - B).
(a) Evaluate integral cos^2 x dx.
(b) Evaluate integral sin^2 x dx.
(c) Evaluate integral 2 cos 3x cos x dx (use 2 cos A cos B = cos(A+B) + cos(A-B)).
(d) State the identity used in part (c).
questions.answer:
(a) integral cos^2 x dx = integral (1 + cos 2x)/2 dx = x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + C.
(b) integral sin^2 x dx = integral (1 - cos 2x)/2 dx = x/2 - (sin 2x)/4 + C.
(c) 2 cos 3x cos x = cos 4x + cos 2x, so integral 2 cos 3x cos x dx = (sin 4x)/4 + (sin 2x)/2 + C.
(d) 2 cos A cos B = cos(A + B) + cos(A - B).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Choosing a method depends on the form of the integrand: a product of unlike functions suggests parts; a numerator that is the derivative of the denominator suggests substitution; a proper rational function suggests partial fractions; a quadratic form suggests a standard special integral.
(a) Which method suits integral x log x dx, and what is its value?
(b) Which method suits integral (2x)/(x^2 + 7) dx, and what is its value?
(c) Which method suits integral dx/(x^2 + 9)?
(d) Which method suits integral dx/[(x - 1)(x - 3)]?
questions.answer:
(a) Integration by PARTS (algebraic times log). u = log x, dv = x dx: integral x log x dx = (x^2/2) log x - x^2/4 + C.
(b) SUBSTITUTION t = x^2 + 7 (f'/f form): integral 2x/(x^2 + 7) dx = log (x^2 + 7) + C.
(c) SPECIAL/standard integral: integral dx/(x^2 + 9) = (1/3) tan^-1 (x/3) + C.
(d) PARTIAL FRACTIONS (distinct linear factors x - 1 and x - 3).
questions.explanation: Match each integrand to parts / substitution / standard / partial fractions.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student integrates several functions and must verify results by differentiation. Recall integral e^x dx = e^x + C, integral (1/x) dx = log |x| + C, and integral cos x dx = sin x + C.
(a) Verify that integral 2x dx = x^2 + C by differentiation.
(b) A student writes integral (1/x) dx = -1/x^2 + C. Is this correct? Explain.
(c) Evaluate integral (e^x + 1/x) dx.
(d) Why does differentiating any correct indefinite integral return the integrand?
questions.answer:
(a) d/dx (x^2 + C) = 2x, which is the integrand, so integral 2x dx = x^2 + C is correct.
(b) No. -1/x^2 is the derivative of 1/x, not its integral. The correct result is integral (1/x) dx = log |x| + C (check: d/dx log|x| = 1/x).
(c) integral (e^x + 1/x) dx = e^x + log |x| + C.
(d) Because integration is defined as the inverse of differentiation: if integral f dx = F + C with F' = f, then differentiating F + C gives back f, the integrand.
questions.explanation: Verify by differentiating; correct 1/x integral; inverse relationship.
